findings.title: First offline access token is encoded as an online session
findings.body: createTokenResponse calls createClientAccessToken, which stamps the jti session-type from userSession.isOffline(), before generateRefreshToken() and before the online session may be deleted. On the first offline_access response the login session is still online at that point, so the prefix is online (on…). Lines 116-120 then issue an offline refresh token and, when the FIRST_OFFLINE_ACCESS note is set, remove that online user session. Offline sessions live in a separate store but keep the same session id, so today's validation only finds the session by falling back from online to offline. The prefix names the store that no longer holds the session. Callers that use it to pick a single store, which is the stated reason for encoding session type, will miss the session and reject the access token returned with that first offline refresh token. ResourceOwnerPasswordCredentialsGrantType has the same order and is stricter: generateAccessToken() at line 139 runs first, then any offline refresh token causes removeUserSession at lines 142-146, not only the first-offline-access case. Later refreshes are fine because the loaded session is already offline. No test issues an offline_access token and checks the session-type characters.

findings.title: Constructor null-checks grantType instead of rawTokenId
findings.body: The fourth Objects.requireNonNull still passes grantType, with the message Null rawTokenId not allowed. A null rawTokenId is accepted. encodeTokenId concatenates the raw id with string +, so null becomes the literal suffix :null. Every such token shares that jti suffix, so ids are no longer unique, and the constructor does not enforce the invariant it claims.

findings.title: Access-token id matcher is inverted and reads the wrong slice
findings.body: isAccessTokenId is what expectCodeToToken, expectRefresh, expectDeviceCodeToToken, and expectAuthReqIdToToken now use to assert the new jti. The grant shortcut is characters at indexes 4 and 5 of the six-character prefix (onrtac is ac), but the matcher uses substring(3, 5), which is ta for that id. The condition is also backwards: it returns false when that slice equals the expected shortcut. For every built-in shortcut these helpers pass, the wrong slice is not equal to the expected value, so the inverted check does not fire and any id with a colon and a UUID suffix passes, including the na fallback used when GRANT_TYPE was never set. The new assertions therefore do not fail if grant encoding is missing or wrong, and they never check session type or token type. A prefix shorter than 5 characters throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException from the matcher instead of a mismatch.

findings.title: getShortcut() has no default and breaks existing grant factories at startup
findings.body: OAuth2GrantTypeFactory is an existing extension SPI, and getShortcut() was added as a new abstract method with no default implementation. DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit loads every OAuth2GrantTypeFactory and calls getShortcut(). A custom grant factory built against the previous interface throws AbstractMethodError there, and Keycloak fails to start. A default method that returns a stable two-character fallback would keep existing providers loading.

findings.title: Grant shortcuts are not constrained to the two-character encoding
findings.body: Decoding assumes every grant shortcut is exactly two characters and contains no colon, so the prefix is always six characters and the first colon separates the raw id. getShortcut() is documented as usually like a 3-letter shortcut, and postInit only checks that the two maps end up the same size. A unique shortcut of any other length is stored, encodeTokenId writes it into the jti, and getTokenContextFromTokenId then throws IllegalArgumentException because the prefix length is not 6. That exception text says the token id is expected to have length 6, but the check is only on the prefix; a valid id is six characters, a colon, and a UUID, so the message is wrong. The lazy reload in getShortcutByGrantType and getGrantTypeByShortcut, meant for grants deployed after startup, inserts the new shortcut with no length check and no collision check, so a duplicate shortcut overwrites another grant and later tokens decode as the wrong grant type.

findings.title: setFormParams leaves the cached grant type stale
findings.body: Context snapshots grant_type from the constructor form parameters, and getGrantType() returns that field. setFormParams replaces formParams but does not update grantType. A caller that uses this public setter to change the request parameters after construction will encode the original grant type, or na if the original map had no grant_type, rather than the grant type actually being processed. The getter should read the current form parameters, or the setter should refresh the cached value.
